flow.kid: Take 2 beans from each bowl. Put 3 in Bowl B. Count. Do this for 15 rounds or until a bowl is empty.

ask.q: What is happening to Bowl B when you take 2 and add 3?
good: It is getting fuller by one bean every round.
Nature is giving back more than we take.

flow.parent: Expect Bowl A to be empty at the end of round 10. Bowl B grows by one bean a round and has 35 beans after round 15. If your child skips the adding, the counts will not match, so watch that step.

flow.do: Test 2. Reset both bowls to 20 beans. This time take 4 beans from each bowl every round, then add 3 to Bowl B. Go on for up to 15 rounds. Write the count after each round. At the end, say how many beans Bowl B has left after round 15.
flow.say: Now take 4 each round. Bowl B still gets 3. Is it going up, staying the same or going down? By how much each round?
flow.kid: Reset. Take 4 beans from each bowl. Put 3 in Bowl B. Count after each round.

ask.q: Bowl B still has beans at round 15. Is it safe?
good: No. The bowl goes down by one bean every round, so the beans will run out later.
It looks fine now, but the speed of taking is bigger than the speed of giving.

flow.parent: Bowl A is empty at the end of round 5. Bowl B goes down by one bean each round and has 5 beans left after round 15. If you went on, the bowl would be empty in round 17. That is a slow slide, and it is easy to miss if you stop early.

flow.do: Test 3. Reset both bowls to 20 beans. Take 6 beans from each bowl every round, then add 3 to Bowl B. Write the count after each round, and note the round in which each bowl is empty.
flow.say: Now take 6 each round. Bowl B still gets 3. What do you think will happen this time?
flow.kid: Reset. Take 6 beans from each bowl. Put 3 in Bowl B. Count after each round.
flow.parent: Bowl A is empty in round 4. Bowl B is empty in round 6, because 5 beans are left when 6 are needed. Bowl B lasts longer than Bowl A, so nature's giving did help. It could not keep up with the taking.

flow.do: Look at the results table together. Find one test in which Bowl B never ran out. Find one in which Bowl B ran out. Ask which number made the difference, and what that number was compared with. Then ask what Bowl A would need, to behave like Bowl B.
flow.say: In which test did Bowl B never run out? What was different about the taking and the giving back? What would Bowl A need so that it could last as well?
flow.kid: Look at your table. When did Bowl B last? Compare the beans taken with the beans added.

ask.q: What was the difference between the tests in which Bowl B lasted and the tests in which it ran out?
good: Taking 3 or fewer beans a round let Bowl B last, because 3 are added.
When we took more than we added, Bowl B shrank.
It was the speed of taking compared with the speed of giving back.

ask.q: Coal is made again in swamps, but only after millions of years. Which bowl is it like, and how many beans does the sky add?
good: It is like Bowl A, because the adding is far too slow to wait for.
The adding is so tiny that it is nearly nothing in a human life.

flow.parent: The answer to look for is that the same bowl can last or run out. It depends on how fast we take compared with how fast it fills. A source is renewable only while the taking is slower than the giving back.

flow.do: Say what this test cannot tell us. Real forests and wells do not get exactly 3 beans every round. Rain is sometimes more and sometimes less. Ask what the child would change in the test to make it more like a real forest, and write one idea.
flow.say: In this game the sky gave exactly 3 beans every round. Is a real forest like that? What would you change so that the game is more like a real forest or a real well?
flow.kid: Write one change that would make the game more like a real forest.

ask.q: What would you change in the test to make it more like a real well?
good: Add a different number of beans in different rounds, because rain changes.
Add a bad year with no beans, to match a drought.
Make a bowl for each village and let them share.

flow.think: If nature gives back a different amount every year, how would a village know how much it is safe to take?

experiments.title: The sun-catcher test: does black catch more of the Sun?
experiments.question: Two tumblers of water sit in the same sunlight for half an hour. One is wrapped in black paper and one in shiny foil. Which water is warmer?
experiments.predict: Before putting them in the Sun, guess which tumbler will be warmer, or if they will be the same. Say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: Both tumblers are the same size, hold the same amount of water from the same jug and start at the same temperature. They sit side by side on the same sill for the same 30 minutes. The only thing that differs is the wrapping. If you can, do the test twice and swap the tumblers' places the second time, because one place on a sill can be sunnier than another.

materials.item: 2 steel tumblers of the same size
black paper or black cloth, and sticky tape
kitchen foil
a thermometer, or a clean finger
a clean spoon, a measuring cup and a clock or phone timer

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Write what you expected, what you found and the reason. Say how you know both tumblers had the same sunlight.
experiments.context: In this experiment you warm water in the sun in a black tumbler and a foil tumbler. You find out how a surface can catch the Sun's energy as heat. It needs a sunny day, so it is an extra and not part of the main path.

setup.art: A steel tumbler wrapped in black paper beside a steel tumbler wrapped in shiny foil.
setup.caption: 1. Wrap one tumbler in black paper and one in foil with the shiny side out.

setup.art: A measuring cup pouring 150 millilitres of water into each tumbler from one jug.
setup.caption: 2. Pour the same amount of water into each from one jug.

setup.art: Two wrapped tumblers side by side on a sunny window sill with a phone timer beside them.
setup.caption: 3. Put them side by side in direct sunlight for 30 minutes.

setup.art: A thermometer in a tumbler of water with a hand writing numbers on a table.
setup.caption: 4. Measure each tumbler's water and write the numbers.

flow.do: Find a sunny window sill, balcony or terrace wall that gets direct sunlight at about 11 am to 1 pm. Wrap one steel tumbler in black paper or black cloth, held on with tape. Wrap the other in kitchen foil with the shiny side out. Put 150 millilitres of tap water from one jug into each. Take the temperature of each, and write it down.
flow.say: We have two tumblers that look different. Which one will catch more of the Sun? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Wrap one tumbler in black paper and one in foil. Pour the same amount of water into each. Write the starting temperature.
flow.parent: Use the same jug of water, so that both tumblers start at the same temperature. If you have no thermometer, dip a clean finger in each, and rank the tumblers by touch.

flow.do: Ask for the prediction and the reason. Write both before the tumblers go into the Sun.
flow.say: Which tumbler will be warmer after half an hour in the Sun? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess which tumbler will be warmer. Write why you think so.
flow.parent: Do not say who is right. Children often guess both will be the same, which is a good thing to test.

flow.do: Put both tumblers side by side on the sunny sill, with the same side facing the window. Start a timer for 30 minutes.
flow.say: Put them next to each other, so that both get the same sunlight. Now we wait for half an hour.
flow.kid: Put both tumblers side by side in the Sun. Start the timer.
flow.wait: Leave the tumblers in the sun for 30 minutes

flow.do: After 30 minutes, take the temperature of each tumbler's water, stirring gently with a clean spoon first. Write both numbers. Work out how many degrees each has warmed. If you have no thermometer, dip a clean finger in each and say which feels warmer.
flow.say: Which tumbler is warmer? How many degrees did each one warm?
flow.kid: Measure each tumbler's water. Which is warmer? By how many degrees?

ask.q: Why was the black tumbler warmer, if both got the same sunlight?
good: Black takes in most of the sunlight and turns it into heat.
Shiny foil bounces much of the sunlight away.

flow.parent: On a clear day, expect the black tumbler to be about 3 to 8 degrees warmer than the foil one. On a hazy day the gap may be only 1 or 2 degrees. If so, try again on a clearer day. If both are the same, check that both were in direct sunlight and not partly in shade.

flow.do: Say what this test cannot tell us. It shows that a black surface catches more of the Sun's warmth than a shiny one. It does not say how much sunlight reaches your city on other days. Ask how a solar water heater might use this idea.
flow.say: A solar water heater on a roof has a black surface. Why do you think that is?
flow.kid: Why would a solar water heater be black inside?

ask.q: Where in your neighbourhood have you seen black surfaces or shiny surfaces used for heat?
good: Black pipes and tanks on roofs catch heat.
Shiny foil in a lunch box helps to keep heat in or out.

flow.think: If clouds covered the Sun for a week, which of your energy sources would you still have?

experiments.safety: Never look at the Sun. Tumblers left in strong sun can get hot, so touch one with a fingertip first and lift them with a cloth.

activities.title: Home energy source hunt: where does each thing get its energy?
activities.context: In this activity you walk round your home and find what each machine, light and body gets its energy from. You then sort the sources by how quickly nature makes them again.

materials.item: paper and a pencil
a clipboard or a hard book to write on

schedule.what: Walk round the home, list the sources, then sort them by how fast nature makes them again.

activities.record: A page with three columns: comes back in days to a few years, takes millions of years, not sure. Write each source in a column.

setup.art: A child with a clipboard looking at a ceiling fan, a gas stove and a phone charger in a home.
setup.caption: 1. Walk round your home and list eight things that use energy.

setup.art: A page with the heading energy source next to a list of things, with arrows from things to sources.
setup.caption: 2. For each thing, write its energy source.

setup.art: A page divided into three columns: days to years, millions of years, not sure.
setup.caption: 3. Sort the sources into the three columns.

flow.do: Walk through the kitchen, a bedroom and the balcony or doorway. List eight things that use energy. Include a light, a fan and the kitchen burner. Add something with a plug, something with a battery, and one living being such as the child or a plant.
flow.say: Let us find eight things in our home that use energy. What can you find?
flow.kid: Walk round the home. Write eight things that use energy.
flow.parent: Include the child's own body and a plant on the list. They are using energy too, and their source is easy to find.

flow.do: For each thing, ask where its energy comes from, and write the source beside it. For a plug thing, write electricity, and then ask where the electricity came from. For the child, write food. Mark anything you do not know with a question mark.
flow.say: Where does the fan get its energy? And where does that energy come from before it? Let us follow it back as far as we can.
flow.kid: Write each thing's energy source. Follow it back one step.

ask.q: Where does the electricity in the wall come from?
good: From a power station, which may burn coal or use water, wind or sunlight.
I do not know yet. We can find out from the bill or the electricity board.

flow.parent: Most children will stop at the wall socket. Gently ask where the wire goes. In many cities the electricity bill or the state electricity board's website lists the mix.

flow.do: Draw three columns on a page. Write 'comes back in days to a few years', 'takes millions of years' and 'not sure'. Put each source in a column. Cooking fuel in a cylinder, petrol and coal go in the middle column. Food, firewood, sunlight and wind go in the first. Electricity goes under not sure, until you find out where it comes from.
flow.say: Which column has the most things? Which sources are you not sure about?
flow.kid: Sort each source into a column. Put a question mark on any you are not sure about.

ask.q: Why does electricity not fit in a column by itself?
good: Electricity is a way of carrying energy. It can come from coal or from the wind.
We need to ask where it was made.

flow.think: If you could only keep the sources from the first column, what in your home would change?

activities.title: A rope of time: how old is the sunlight in each source?
activities.context: In this activity you lay out a 3 metre string as a rope of time, where 1 centimetre stands for a million years. You mark when coal was made and when people started burning it, and see how small our part is.

materials.item: a 3 metre string, a ball of wool or a strip of paper tape
a tape measure or a ruler
sticky notes or small paper flags
a fine-pointed pencil

schedule.what: Lay out the rope, mark the old times, then try to mark the 250 years of burning coal.

activities.record: Draw the rope as a line on paper and write the marks along it with their ages. Write how long the 250 years would be if you drew it.

setup.art: A 3 metre string laid along a hallway floor with a note at one end saying today.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the string. One end is today. Each centimetre is a million years.

setup.art: Paper flags at 66 centimetres, 230 centimetres and between 250 and 300 centimetres along the string.
setup.caption: 2. Mark the end of the dinosaurs, the first dinosaurs and the coal swamps.

setup.art: A fine pencil point on the string at the today end, with a magnifying glass over it.
setup.caption: 3. Mark the 250 years of burning coal. It is smaller than the pencil dot.

flow.do: Lay the string along a hall or across a room. Tape one end down and write 'today' on a note there. Explain that 1 centimetre on the string stands for 1 million years. So 3 metres stands for 300 million years. Mark the ends with a note each.
flow.say: This string is a rope of time. One centimetre means a million years. The whole string means 300 million years. Where would you put the dinosaurs?
flow.kid: Lay the string out. One end is today. Each centimetre is a million years.
flow.parent: If the hall is too short, fold the string back on itself like a snake, or use a longer wool ball and mark with ink. The sums are the same.

flow.do: Place paper flags along the string. Put the end of the dinosaurs, about 66 million years ago, at 66 centimetres. Put the first dinosaurs, about 230 million years ago, at 230 centimetres. Put the coal swamps of India, roughly 250 to 300 million years ago, at the far end, between 250 and 300 centimetres. Put the first people of our own kind, roughly 300,000 years ago, at 3 millimetres from today.
flow.say: Where do you think the coal swamps go? Were they before or after the dinosaurs? Where are the first people?
flow.kid: Put the flags in place. Where is the coal? Where are we?

ask.q: Is the coal older than the first dinosaurs, or younger?
good: Older. The coal swamps are near the far end of the rope.
The coal is about as old as the first dinosaurs or a bit older.

flow.parent: Dates are rounded and different books give slightly different numbers. The point is the size of the gaps.

flow.do: Now ask the child to mark where the 250 years of burning coal would go. It starts at the today end. 250 years is 0.00025 centimetres. That is 2.5 micrometres, and a micrometre is a thousandth of a millimetre. Show a pencil dot. Even a fine pencil makes a dot about 0.3 millimetres wide, which is 300 micrometres. The dot is more than 100 times wider than the 250 years. Ask what that tells us.
flow.say: How long is 250 years on our rope? Try to make a mark that small. Is it bigger or smaller than your pencil dot?
flow.kid: Try to mark 250 years on the rope. Is your mark too big?

ask.q: What does it mean that we are burning coal in a blink on this rope?
good: We are using in a tiny moment what took a very long time to make.
The coal cannot be made again in any time that people can plan for.

flow.parent: Use a fine pencil and a ruler with millimetres to see that the dot is much wider than the 250 years. The maths: 250 divided by 1,000,000 is 0.00025 centimetres, and one centimetre is 10,000 micrometres, so 0.00025 times 10,000 is 2.5 micrometres.

flow.do: Ask the child to say what the rope shows about which sources are renewable and which are not. Then ask where rice, firewood and the wind would sit on the rope.
flow.say: Where would last season's rice go on the rope? And firewood from a thirty-year-old tree? And the wind that blew this morning?
flow.kid: Where do rice, firewood and wind go on the rope?

ask.q: Why do rice, firewood and wind all sit so close to today?
good: The sunlight in them is only months or years old.
Their sunlight came back very recently, so they can be made again soon.

flow.think: If we call coal old sunlight, who first saved it?

activities.title: The watt hunt: which things in the house use the most energy?
activities.context: In this activity you read the watts on the labels of things in your home. You work out how much energy each one uses in a day, and find that the hungriest things are not always the ones you expect.

materials.item: paper and a pencil
a phone with a torch, to read small labels

schedule.what: Find the watts on six things, estimate their hours, and work out which uses the most energy in a day.

activities.record: A table with four columns: the thing, its watts, its hours in a day and watts times hours. Circle the biggest number.
activities.safety: Read the labels only. Do not open any machine. Do not pull a plug with wet hands.

setup.art: A child with a phone torch reading the small print on the back of a ceiling fan and a mixie.
setup.caption: 1. Find the label that gives the watts. Try a bulb, a fan, a mixie, an iron and a charger.

setup.art: A table with columns for the thing, watts, hours in a day and energy.
setup.caption: 2. Write the watts and a guess for the hours in a day.

setup.art: A page with two bars of different lengths for a fan and an iron.
setup.caption: 3. Multiply watts by hours and compare.

flow.do: Find six things that use electricity. Read the watts on each, from a label on the machine or its box. Try an LED bulb, a ceiling fan, a mixie, an iron or a phone charger, a television and a fridge. If a label shows volts and amps, multiply them to get watts. If there is no label, use these numbers: bulb 9, fan 60, mixie 500, iron 1,000, charger 10, television 80, fridge 150.
flow.say: Which do you think uses the most energy in one day? A bulb that is on all evening, a fan on all night or an iron that is on for ten minutes?
flow.kid: Find the watts on six things. Write them in a table.
flow.parent: Watts say how fast a thing uses energy, not how much it uses in a day. A big number for a short time can be less than a small number for a long time. Do not give the answer yet.

flow.do: Ask the child to guess how many hours each thing is on in a day. Write the guess. Then work out watts times hours for each, and call the answer 'watt-hours'. For example, a 60 watt fan on for 10 hours uses 60 times 10, which is 600 watt-hours.
flow.say: A fan of 60 watts is on for 10 hours. Multiply 60 by 10. How many watt-hours is that?
flow.kid: For each thing, multiply watts by hours. Write the answer.

ask.q: Which thing uses the most energy in a day, and which uses the least?
good: The thing with the biggest watts times hours, which is often a fan or a fridge, not an iron.
A thing with large watts can use less in a day if it is on for a short time.

flow.parent: Typical results: bulb 9 watts for 5 hours is 45 watt-hours. Iron 1,000 watts for 10 minutes is roughly 170. Fan 60 watts for 10 hours is 600. Fridge 150 watts working about 7 hours in a day is about 1,050.

flow.do: Explain that a unit on the electricity bill is 1,000 watt-hours. Work out how many days the whole list would take to make 1 unit. Then ask what the family could change to use less in a day, and how many watt-hours that would save.
flow.say: A unit on the bill is 1,000 watt-hours. If we switch off the fan for 2 hours a day, how many watt-hours do we save?
flow.kid: A unit is 1,000 watt-hours. How many do you save by switching the fan off for 2 hours?

ask.q: What small change would save the most watt-hours in your home?
good: Switching off a fan or lights in an empty room for several hours.
Using a lid or a pressure cooker, because it saves gas as well.

flow.parent: A 60 watt fan switched off for 2 hours saves 120 watt-hours. Over a month of 30 days that is 3,600 watt-hours, which is more than 3 units.

flow.do: Ask whether the hungriest thing is also the one that matters most to the family. Listen for answers about fridges, fans in heat, and iron for school clothes. Say that using less is a choice about what is worth the energy, not only a sum.
flow.say: The fridge uses a lot, but it keeps the food from spoiling. Is it worth it? How would you decide?
flow.kid: Which thing is worth the energy it uses? Why?
flow.think: Is there anything in your home that you could do without, and anything you could not?

activities.title: The dam meeting: who gets to decide?
activities.context: In this activity a family acts out a village meeting about a new dam. Each person speaks for someone who gains or loses, including the river and the forest, and then everyone decides.

materials.item: 6 small slips of paper and a pen
a cup to draw slips from
a timer

schedule.what: Draw roles, give one-minute speeches, then vote and talk about what each person would change.

activities.record: Draw a table with the headings 'who gains', 'who loses' and 'who spoke for them'. Fill it in after the vote.

setup.art: Six paper slips folded in a cup, each with a role written in a child's handwriting.
setup.caption: 1. Write six roles on slips and draw one each.

setup.art: A family seated in a circle with a timer on the floor, one person speaking with a hand raised.
setup.caption: 2. Each person speaks for one minute as the person on their slip.

setup.art: A hand dropping a bean into one of two bowls marked yes and no.
setup.caption: 3. Vote with a bean, then say what would change your vote.

flow.do: Write one role on each of six slips. One is a farmer downstream who needs water. One is a city family who needs electricity. One is a forest elder whose village lies behind the dam. One is a fisher who catches fish in the river. One is an engineer who has built dams before. The last one speaks for the river and the forest animals. If there are fewer than six people, use fewer slips. Each person draws one and keeps it secret for now.
flow.say: A big dam is planned on a river. Each of us will speak for someone different. We will not choose our own role. Draw a slip.
flow.kid: Draw a slip. You will speak as that person in a moment.
flow.parent: Make sure the one who speaks for the river is included. Beings who cannot come to the meeting are easy to forget. Children aged 6 to 10 often enjoy this role most.

flow.do: Give each person one minute to say what they gain and what they lose if the dam is built. Use the timer. Listen without arguing. After each speech, ask one question to that person.
flow.say: In one minute, tell us what you gain or lose if the dam is built. Speak as your person would speak.
flow.kid: Speak for one minute as your person. Tell what you gain and what you lose.

ask.q: Who gains the most, and who loses the most?
good: The city family gains electricity. The forest village and the river lose the most.
Answers vary. A strong answer names several groups, including the river and animals.

flow.do: Everyone discusses for three minutes. Then each person votes by dropping a bean in a bowl marked yes or no. Say that you may vote as yourself and not as the person on your slip. Count the beans together.
flow.say: Now vote as yourself. Do you want the dam to be built? What would change your vote?
flow.kid: Vote with a bean. Then say what would change your vote.

ask.q: What other choices could the village have, so that nobody loses so much?
good: A smaller dam, or wind and solar power instead.
Using less electricity in the city.
Paying and moving the families, with their say.

flow.parent: There is no right vote. Do not tell the child which side is right. Both sides have real arguments.

flow.do: Ask who in the room was easiest to forget, and how the decision might change if that person had a vote. Write the three groups on the table: who gains, who loses and who spoke for them.
flow.say: Who was hardest to speak for? How could a village hear someone who cannot come to the meeting?
flow.kid: Fill in the table of who gains, who loses and who spoke for them.
flow.think: Should a river or a forest have a say about what happens to them?

activities.title: Lid on, lid off: does a lid save gas?
activities.context: In this activity you boil water in two pans at once on two burners, one with a lid and one without. You find out how much sooner the lid brings the water to the boil, which means less gas burnt.

materials.item: 2 steel pans of the same size, and one lid that fits
a two-burner gas stove
a measuring jug
a timer or phone stopwatch

schedule.what: An adult boils 500 millilitres of water in each pan, one with the lid on, while the child times each.

activities.record: Write the time at which each pan first boiled strongly. Write who won, and by how many seconds.
activities.safety: An adult lights the stove and moves the pans. Keep the child at arm's length from the flame and steam. Open a window for fresh air. Lift the lid away from your face.

setup.art: Two same-sized steel pans on a two-burner stove, one with a lid and one open, with equal flames.
setup.caption: 1. Put the same amount of water in two pans. Put the lid on one.

setup.art: A child holding a phone stopwatch and watching from a safe distance, with an adult at the stove.
setup.caption: 2. An adult lights both burners together. The child times from lighting.

setup.art: Two pans with large bubbles all over the water, and a hand writing times on a page.
setup.caption: 3. Write the time when each pan first boils strongly all over.

flow.do: An adult measures 500 millilitres of cold tap water into each of the two pans. Put the lid on one pan. Set both flames to the same medium level. Do not light them yet. Ask for the prediction and reason.
flow.say: Two pans have the same water. One has a lid, and one does not. Which will boil first? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess which pan will boil first. Write why.
flow.parent: Choose pans of the same size and metal. If you have only one lid, that is enough. The lid pan is the one being tested.

flow.do: The adult lights both burners together. The child starts the stopwatch. Watch until bubbles rise all over the water in each pan, and note each time. Turn both flames off at once. Leave the pans where no one will touch them until they are cool.
flow.say: Press start when the flames light. Tell us when the water in each pan is bubbling all over.
flow.kid: Start the stopwatch when the stove is lit. Write the time when each pan bubbles all over.
flow.parent: Usually the pan with the lid boils about 1 to 2 minutes sooner, though the size of the gap depends on your stove. If the two times are within 20 seconds, the two burners may have different flames. Swap the lid to the other burner tomorrow and try again. If your stove has only one burner, test the two pans on two days, with the same flame and the same water. Never lift the lid with your face over the pan.

flow.do: Compare the two times. Ask why the lid made a difference, and where the heat goes in the pan with no lid. Ask the child how much fuel the family could save in a month if a lid were used every time.
flow.say: Which pan boiled first, and by how much? Where do you think the heat went in the pan with no lid?
flow.kid: Which pan boiled first? How many seconds sooner?

ask.q: Why does a lid make the water boil sooner?
good: It keeps the hot air and steam in, so the heat stays in the pan.
Without a lid, much of the heat escapes with the steam.

flow.parent: Remember to tell the child this test cannot say how much gas the lid saved in your home. It only shows that the lid makes the heating faster. A lid is one small way of using less.

projects.title: A week of less: how much energy can our home save?
projects.context: In this project your family counts the lights and fans left on in empty rooms for one week. You work out how much energy a few simple habits save, and notice if the saving gets spent on something else.

materials.item: a notebook for a week of notes
a pencil
the electricity bill or meter, if you can read it
sticky notes to put beside switches

schedule.what: Make a list of the lights and fans in the home, with their watts and a guess of the hours each is on in a day.
At about 8 pm, count the lights and fans on in empty rooms. This is the starting count.
Put a sticky note beside each switch. Agree one rule, such as switching off when leaving a room. Count again at 8 pm.
Keep the rule. Count again at 8 pm and write the number.
Keep the rule. Count again at 8 pm and write the number.
Keep the rule. Count again, and add one more habit that the family chooses, such as a lid on the pot.
Work out the watt-hours saved, compare days 2 and 6, and talk about what changed.

projects.record: A table with one row for each evening. Add a column for the lights and fans on in empty rooms and a column for the watt-hours wasted. Draw a bar for each evening. End with three short lines about what you expected, what you found and the reason.

setup.art: A home floor plan drawn on paper with a bulb or fan marked in each room and its watts beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Day 1: draw the rooms and mark each light and fan with its watts.

setup.art: A child at 8 pm looking into an empty bedroom where a fan and a light are still on.
setup.caption: 2. Days 2 to 6: at the same time each evening, count what is on in empty rooms.

setup.art: A sticky note saying 'last out, switch off' on a wall beside a light switch.
setup.caption: 3. Day 3: put a note beside each switch and agree the family rule.

setup.art: A bar chart with six bars that get shorter after the third bar.
setup.caption: 4. Day 7: draw a bar for each evening and compare.

flow.do: Walk through the home with a notebook. List each light and fan. Write its watts, from its label or from these numbers: LED bulb 9, tube light 36, fan 60. Guess how many hours each is on in a day. Work out watts times hours for each. Add them up for the whole home.
flow.say: How many lights and fans do we have? How many hours do you think each is on? Let us add up the watt-hours.
flow.kid: List every light and fan in your home. Write the watts and a guess for the hours.
flow.parent: You are only building a picture of where the energy goes. A rough guess is good enough. If your meter is easy to read, write the reading at the same time each day too.

flow.do: At about 8 pm, walk round and count the lights and fans that are on in rooms where nobody is. Write the number and the watts they add up to. Do not switch anything off yet, and do not blame anyone.
flow.say: Let us count how many lights and fans are on with nobody in the room. Write the number. We are only looking today.
flow.kid: Count the lights and fans on in empty rooms. Write the number.
flow.parent: This is a count, not a test of who is careless. A child can do it alone with a torch if they like.
flow.wait: Count at the same time each evening

flow.do: On day 3, put a sticky note beside each switch that says 'last one out, switch off'. Agree the rule together. Count the lights and fans on in empty rooms at 8 pm on days 3, 4 and 5 and write each number. Keep the rule the same on all three days.
flow.say: From today, the last person out of a room switches off the light and the fan. Let us see what the count does.
flow.kid: Put notes by the switches. Keep the rule. Count at 8 pm and write the number.

ask.q: What happens to the count when everyone follows the rule?
good: It goes down, because fewer things are left on.
It may go up some days, when someone forgets, and that is useful to see.

flow.parent: If the family forgets on a day, write the number anyway. Honest counts are more useful than neat ones.

flow.do: On day 6, count again. Then ask the family to choose one more habit for a day. It could be a lid on the pot, or the fan on only when someone is in the room. Write down which one.
flow.say: What is one more small thing our family could do to use less energy? Let us try it for today.
flow.kid: Count again. Choose one more habit and write it down.

ask.q: What is one more habit that would not make anyone's day harder?
good: A lid on the pot, because it saves gas.
Fan off when nobody is in the room.
A full load in the washing machine.

flow.do: On day 7, put the evening counts in a table. Work out the watt-hours wasted each evening. Multiply the watts of the things left on by 2 hours, a fair guess for how long they stay on. Draw a bar for each evening. Compare days 2 and 6. Then ask the family if they used the saving for something else, such as the television or the air conditioner.
flow.say: How did the counts change from day 2 to day 6? How many watt-hours did we save? Did anything else use more energy, to make up for it?
flow.kid: Draw a bar for each evening. Compare the first and the last. Write what you notice.

ask.q: Did the family use more energy somewhere else during the week?
good: Maybe the television was on more, or a second fan.
Saving in one place can free energy to be used in another place, and that is worth watching.

flow.think: If everyone in your street did the same for a year, how much coal would stay in the ground?

challenges.title: A box that keeps food hot with no fuel
challenges.context: This is a design problem. Gas is burnt to heat food. You build an insulated box that keeps hot water hot for two hours with no fuel, so that less gas is needed to cook.
challenges.problem: Keep 500 millilitres of hot water in a lidded steel container as warm as you can for 2 hours. Use no fuel, no electricity and nothing you must buy. Compare it with the same container left on the counter. There is more than one good answer.
constraints: Use only things you can find at home, such as a cardboard box, newspaper, old cloth and foil.
Nothing may be plugged in or heated after the water is poured.
The box must close, and the container must be easy to take out.
Test your box against a container of the same size left on the counter, and write both temperatures.
materials: 2 lidded steel containers or two steel bowls with plates for lids
a cardboard box with a lid, large enough for one container with 5 centimetres of space around it
old newspaper, an old towel or a cloth, and kitchen foil
a thermometer, or a clean spoon to test warmth with the back of the wrist
hot water from a kettle, poured by an adult
paper and a pencil to record the temperatures

setup.art: Two steel containers side by side, one on a counter and one inside a cardboard box packed with newspaper.
setup.caption: 1. Fill two containers with hot water. Leave one on the counter and put one in a box.

setup.art: A cardboard box lined with foil and stuffed with crumpled newspaper around a steel container.
setup.caption: 2. Try the usual way: pack the box around the container with newspaper or cloth.

setup.art: A box inside a second bigger box, with a gap between the two filled with crumpled paper.
setup.caption: 3. Try a creative way: a box in a box with an air gap, or a foil lining and a cushion on top.

setup.art: A hand holding a thermometer in a container of warm water, and a page of temperatures beside it.
setup.caption: 4. After 2 hours, measure each container and compare.

flow.do: An adult pours 500 millilitres of just-boiled water into each of two containers and puts on the lids. The adult measures the starting temperature of each. Write it down. Put one container on the counter. This is the comparison. Do not touch the water.
flow.say: These two containers have the same water at the same heat. One will stay on the counter. What do you think will happen to its heat in 2 hours? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Write the starting temperature of each container. Leave one on the counter.

ask.q: Where does the heat of the water go when it cools on the counter?
good: It spreads into the air and the table around it.
It moves from the hot water to the cooler things nearby.

flow.parent: Water from a kettle is hot enough to burn. The adult pours and lifts. A hot container also needs a cloth to hold it. If you have no thermometer, use the back of the wrist on the steel outside after the first hour.

flow.do: Build the usual solution first. Stand the second container in the box and pack newspaper or a folded towel all round it and on top. Close the lid. Note what materials you used and how thick the layer is. Put a mark on the box so you know which is which.
flow.say: What do you think keeps the heat in? Which of the materials in the house do you think is best? Try the usual way first.
flow.kid: Pack the container in the box with newspaper or cloth. Close the lid.

ask.q: Why do you think newspaper or cloth keeps heat in better than bare steel?
good: Trapped air does not carry heat well, and paper and cloth hold a lot of air.
A thick layer is harder for the heat to get through.

flow.parent: The usual solutions here are cloth, newspaper and a lid. Count a layer as at least a hand's width.

flow.do: Now try one creative idea of your own. Line the inside with foil. Put a second box around the first with a gap of crumpled paper between them. Put a folded cushion or towel on top. Close it. Write what you changed. Leave both containers for 2 hours.
flow.say: Think of one more way to stop the heat getting out. What will you change? How will you know it is better?
flow.kid: Change something to make the box better. Write what you changed. Leave it for 2 hours.
flow.parent: There is more than one good answer. A box in a box with an air gap, or a box with a cushion on top, are common creative ones. Do not open the box during the wait, because heat escapes each time.
flow.wait: Leave both containers for 2 hours without opening them

flow.do: After 2 hours, an adult opens each container. Measure the water in each one, or dip a clean spoon in each and touch the back of the wrist. Write both. Work out how many degrees each lost. Compare the box with the counter. Then ask how the family could use the box to finish cooking dal or rice with less gas.
flow.say: Which container is warmer? How many degrees did each lose? What did the box do?
flow.kid: Measure both containers. Write how many degrees each lost.

ask.q: What would you change next, to keep the water warm longer?
good: More layers, or a tighter fit so that less air moves.
A lid on the box so that nothing leaks.
Put in less space around the container.

flow.parent: The container in the box should be clearly warmer than the one on the counter, often by 10 degrees or more. Your numbers depend on the box and the room. If both are the same, check that the lid was on and the box was closed. Some families finish cooking in a hay box after bringing food to the boil.

general: Pack a cardboard box tightly with newspaper or old cloth all round and on top of the container.
Wrap the container in a thick towel and put it in a bag or a basket.
Keep the lid on the container, and keep the box closed for the whole time.
creative: Put the container in a box that sits inside a bigger box, with crumpled paper in the gap, so there are two layers of trapped air.
Line the box with foil, shiny side in, so that heat is sent back to the container.
Put in a brick that has sat in the Sun for an hour, wrapped in cloth. It is a second small store of heat that keeps the box warm.
challenges.your_turn: Design your own box and test it against the counter. What did you change that kept the water warmest? How could your family use it to save gas in a month?

challenges.title: Make the Sun's hours do the work: plan a day for a house with solar panels
challenges.context: This is a paper design problem. A house has solar panels that make power only in the daytime, and a small battery. You plan the family's day so that most of the energy is used while the Sun shines.
challenges.problem: A house has solar panels that give about 4 units of electricity between 9 am and 4 pm. A small battery can keep 1 unit for the evening. Anything else used at night comes from the grid, which is mostly coal. Plan the family's day so that no more than 1 unit comes from the grid, and say what you would do on a cloudy day. There is more than one good answer.
constraints: A unit is 1,000 watt-hours. Work out each thing's watt-hours by multiplying its watts by its hours.
The battery holds at most 1 unit. Any night use above that comes from the grid, and you aim for 1 unit or less from the grid.
The fridge must stay on all day and night. About 3 tenths of its use falls in the sun hours and 7 tenths outside them.
Everyone must still get light, food, clean clothes and water.
materials: the fridge: 150 watts, working about 7 hours in a day, which is about 1 unit
4 LED bulbs: 9 watts each, on for 5 hours in the evening
2 fans: 60 watts each, on for 8 hours at night
a water pump: 750 watts, for half an hour
a washing machine: 400 watts, for 1 hour
a television: 80 watts, for 4 hours in the evening

setup.art: A rooftop with a solar panel, a small battery box beside a door, and a Sun shown at noon.
setup.caption: 1. The house has panels for the day and a small battery for the evening.

setup.art: A page with a list of appliances and their watts and hours written beside each.
setup.caption: 2. Write each appliance's watts times hours, in watt-hours.

setup.art: A day drawn as a long strip, with the Sun hours shaded and the evening and night hours unshaded.
setup.caption: 3. Put each job on the strip in the hour you choose.

flow.do: Work out the watt-hours for each appliance. For example, 4 bulbs of 9 watts for 5 hours is 4 times 9 times 5, which is 180 watt-hours. Write them in a list. Add them to find the whole day's energy. Mark each appliance as 'must be at night' or 'could be moved to the sun hours'.
flow.say: How many watt-hours does each thing use? Which can only be used at night, and which could be done at noon?
flow.kid: Work out each appliance's watt-hours. Mark which can move to the sun hours.

ask.q: Which things can wait for the Sun, and which cannot?
good: The pump, the washing machine, the iron and the mixie can be done at noon.
Lights and fans at night cannot move, unless we use less.

flow.parent: Totals in watt-hours: fridge about 1,050, bulbs 180, fans 960, pump 375, mixie 125, iron 250, washing machine 400, television 320. The whole day is about 3,660, which the panels can cover. At night the bulbs, fans, television and the fridge's night share add up to about 2,200. The battery holds 1,000, so about 1,200 would come from the grid. This is what the design has to solve.

flow.do: Try the usual solutions. Move the pump, washing machine, iron and mixie into the sun hours. Run the fridge as normal. Add up what is left for the night. Ask how much would come from the grid after the battery gives its 1 unit. Then decide what to cut so that the grid share is 1 unit or less.
flow.say: If we do the pump, the iron, the mixie and the washing at noon, how much is left for the night? How much must come from the grid?
flow.kid: Move the jobs that can wait into the sun hours. Add up the night use and the grid share.

ask.q: How much comes from the grid after the usual fixes?
good: About 1,200 watt-hours, since the night use is about 2,200 and the battery gives 1,000.
Using one fan and not two saves 480, which brings the grid share to roughly 700, under 1 unit.

flow.do: Now try creative solutions. Think of ways to need less at night, or to store the Sun's work in another way. Could one fan be enough? Could the television be watched at noon? Could water be heated or cooled while the Sun shines? A closed box or an ice tray could keep it until the evening. Write at least two ideas, and work out the watt-hours each one saves.
flow.say: What is a cleverer way to use less at night? Could the Sun's hours cool something for the evening?
flow.kid: Think of two creative ideas. Work out how many watt-hours each one saves.

ask.q: Which creative idea saves the most watt-hours at night?
good: Using one fan and not two saves roughly 480 watt-hours.
Making ice at noon to keep drinks cold saves some fridge use.

flow.do: Plan the cloudy day. Ask what the family would do if the panels made only 1 unit between 9 am and 4 pm. Say which jobs they would do first and which they would give up. Ask where the rest of the energy would come from.
flow.say: On a cloudy day we only get 1 unit. Which jobs would we do first? Where would the rest come from?
flow.kid: Plan a cloudy day. Which jobs do you do first?
flow.think: In India, would a family that has solar panels still need to be joined to the wires of the electricity board? Why?

general: Do the heavy jobs, such as the pump, the iron, the mixie and the washing machine, at noon.
Use LED bulbs and switch off the fans and lights in empty rooms.
Keep the battery for the evening lights and one fan.
creative: Make ice or cool water at noon and use it to keep things cold in the evening, so that the fridge needs less at night.
Cook for the whole day at noon in a box cooker or a hay box and eat the food warm in the evening.
Share the extra noon electricity with neighbours who need it, and borrow some from the grid at night.
challenges.your_turn: Plan your own family's day for a house with solar panels. Which jobs would you move to noon? Which would you give up on a cloudy day? What would you want to know about the real sunlight in your city?

games.title: The Shared Forest: a card game about taking and giving back
games.context: This is a game for 2 to 4 players who share one forest. Everyone secretly chooses how many trees to cut each round. If the forest runs out, everyone loses. If it lasts, whoever has the most wood wins.

setup.art: A steel bowl of 20 beans in the middle of a table, with a small bowl for each player around it.
setup.caption: 1. Put 20 beans in the middle bowl. This is the forest.

setup.art: Four players each holding four cards numbered 0, 1, 2 and 3.
setup.caption: 2. Each player takes a set of four cut cards, numbered 0, 1, 2 and 3.

setup.art: A pile of face-down weather cards beside the forest bowl and a score sheet drawn by hand.
setup.caption: 3. Shuffle the weather cards and put them face down. Draw a score sheet with eight rows.

printables.title: 16 cut cards, four for each of four players
12 weather cards
items: An ordinary year. Nature adds 3 trees.
An ordinary year. Nature adds 3 trees.
An ordinary year. Nature adds 3 trees.
An ordinary year. Nature adds 3 trees.
A good monsoon. Nature adds 4 trees.
A good monsoon. Nature adds 4 trees.
A good monsoon. Nature adds 4 trees.
A very good year, with rain at the right time. Nature adds 5 trees.
A dry spell. Nature adds 2 trees.
A dry spell. Nature adds 2 trees.
The rains failed. Nature adds 0 trees.

printables.title: Score sheet, to copy by hand: eight rows for rounds 1 to 8
items: Round 1. Trees in the forest at the start, trees cut by each player, trees added by the weather, trees in the forest at the end.
Round 8. The same four columns, then each player's wood.

rules: The forest bowl starts with 20 beans. Each bean is a tree. Everyone has a small bowl of their own for the wood they cut.
Each player takes the four cut cards with their own player number. The game lasts 8 rounds.
Each round starts with one minute of talk. Anyone may say what they plan to cut and why. Nobody has to keep a promise.
Then each player puts one cut card face down. Everyone turns their cards over together.
Each player takes that many beans from the forest into their own bowl. This is their wood. If the forest bowl is empty after the cutting, the forest has been lost. Stop the game.
If the forest is still alive, turn over one weather card and add that many beans to the forest bowl. The forest bowl can hold at most 30 beans. Extra beans are put aside.
After round 8, if the forest still has at least 1 bean, count your wood. The player with the most wood wins. If the wood is tied, those players share the win.

If the forest is lost in any round, everyone has lost. Talk about what you each would change next time, then play again. A forest that lasts all 8 rounds is a win for everyone, even if you are not the one with the most wood.

flow.do: Read the rules together. Put 20 beans in the forest bowl. Give each player a set of cut cards and a small bowl. Shuffle the weather cards. Say that the forest is like a well or a wood that nature fills a little each year.
flow.say: We all share one forest. Each round, we each choose how many trees to cut. After we cut, the weather decides how many grow back. If the forest runs out, we all lose.
flow.kid: Put 20 beans in the forest bowl. Take your cut cards. Read the rules.
flow.parent: Cut the cards out and keep them in an envelope for next time. The beans can be any dried bean, button or paper square.

flow.do: Play 8 rounds. In each round, talk for a minute. Then put the cut cards down together and take the wood. Last, turn over a weather card and add trees. Write each round on the score sheet.
flow.say: Talk first. What are you going to cut, and why? Then put down your card and turn them over together.
flow.kid: Talk, then put down a cut card. Turn them over together. Take the wood.

ask.q: Is it better to take a lot early or a little each round?
good: It depends. Taking a lot early can win the wood but can end the forest.
Taking a little keeps the forest alive, but others might get ahead.

ask.q: If you could change one rule, which would you change?
good: Maybe let players share the wood, or let the forest hold more.
Any rule with a reason is good.

flow.parent: Both choices can be reasonable. A group that talks usually keeps the forest alive. A group that does not talk often loses it. Do not tell the child which is better.

flow.do: After round 8, or when the forest is lost, count the wood and the beans left in the forest. Ask the players why the forest did or did not last. Ask what they would change.
flow.say: Did the forest last? What did we do that helped or hurt it?
flow.kid: Count your wood and the forest. Say why the forest lasted or did not.

ask.q: What did you learn about taking and giving back?
good: If we all take too much too fast, the forest ends for everyone.
Talking and agreeing a limit helped the forest last.

flow.think: Who decides how much a village may cut, when the forest belongs to everybody?

worksheets.title: Where does the energy come from? (core)
worksheets.context: This sheet checks three things. You can sort energy sources by how fast they come back. You can say what fossil fuels are made from. You can follow energy back to the Sun.

items.p: Sort each source by how fast nature makes it again.
cats: Comes back in days to a few years
items: Comes back in days to a few years
Comes back in days to a few years
a rice crop in a field
Comes back in days to a few years
rain that fills a river each monsoon
Comes back in days to a few years
items.a: as given
items.why: Sunlight, wind, rice and monsoon rain are made again in days, months or a year. Coal, petrol and natural gas formed from ancient beings over millions of years, so no family can wait for new ones.

items.p: A fuel is something we ____ to let out the energy stored in it.
items.why: Burning lets the stored energy out as heat and light. Sunlight and wind are energy sources, but nothing is burnt, so they are not fuels.

items.p: Match each fuel to what it began as.
pairs: coal
tall plants in a warm swamp
oil
tiny beings that floated in the sea
gobar gas
cow dung eaten by microbes in a closed tank
firewood
a tree that grew in recent years
items.a: as given
items.why: Coal began as swamp plants and oil as tiny sea beings, both millions of years ago. Gobar gas and firewood come from beings who lived lately, so they can be made again soon.

items.p: Most oil was made from the bodies of dinosaurs.
items.why: False. Most oil came from tiny sea beings, too small to see without a microscope, who sank and were buried in mud long ago.

items.p: Both bowls start with 20 beans. Each round, 5 are taken from each. Only Bowl B gets 3 back. Which empties first?
opts: Bowl B
Bowl A
They empty together
items.why: Bowl A has nothing added, so it loses 5 each round and is empty in round 4. Bowl B loses 5 and gains 3, so it falls by 2 each round. It is empty in round 10. Adding helped Bowl B, but not enough.

items.p: A village says its forest is renewable, so it can cut as many trees as it likes. What would you ask them?
items.a: How many trees grow back each year, and how many are cut. If the cutting is faster than the growing, the forest shrinks, however renewable the wood is.
items.why: A strong answer asks about both speeds. Renewable means that nature makes the source again, and it holds only while the taking is slower than the giving back.

items.p: Put these in order, to show how a coal power station lights a bulb. Start with the Sun.
items: the coal is dug up and burnt in a power station
electricity flows along the wires to the bulb
sunlight falls on swamp plants and they grow
the plants die, are buried and are pressed for millions of years
a: sunlight falls on swamp plants and they grow
the plants die, are buried and are pressed for millions of years
the coal is dug up and burnt in a power station
electricity flows along the wires to the bulb
items.why: The sunlight was caught long ago and kept in the coal. The burning lets it out as heat, and the generator turns that into electricity.

items.p: Draw how the Sun makes the wind. Show a sea, a beach and arrows for the air.
items.a: The Sun's rays on both. The land is warmer than the sea. Warm air rising over the land and cooler air moving in from the sea along the ground.
items.why: Land warms faster than sea. Warm air rises, and cooler air slides in to fill the space. That moving air is the wind, so wind is the Sun's work.
items.art: A blank beach, a sea and a Sun, with space to draw arrows.

items.p: Three of these got their energy from the Sun. Which is the odd one out?
opts: Wind
Rain on the hills
A hot spring in the Puga valley
Firewood
items.why: Wind, rain and firewood all come from the Sun's work. The hot spring in the Puga valley in Ladakh is heated by the inside of the Earth.

items.p: Which is a real cost of a big dam?
opts: It adds a lot of soot to the air
It uses up the river for ever
It floods land, and people and other animals lose their homes
items.why: A dam holds back water, so a valley behind it is flooded. Families, forests and fields can be lost. A dam does not burn anything, so it gives out no soot, and the river keeps flowing, though changed.

items.p: A friend says that renewable means harmless. Give one example that shows this is not always true.
items.a: A big dam drowns a valley and blocks fish. Wind turbines can hurt birds, such as great Indian bustards that fly into power lines. Solar parks need a lot of land.
items.why: A good answer names a real cost, such as a drowned valley or a bird killed on a power line. Every way of collecting energy changes the land, the water or the lives nearby.

items.p: A village has money for only one thing this year.

views.who: A mother who cooks on a wood fire (an imagined view)
views.says: Build a biogas tank. The smoke in my kitchen makes my children cough, and gobar gas burns clean.

views.who: A farmer who walks home after dark (an imagined view)
views.says: Put up solar street lights. The lane is dark, and the lamps can run on sunlight stored in a battery.

items.ask: Which would you pick for the village, and what would you want to know first?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer weighs health and safety, asks how many families each choice helps, and notices both choices use energy that comes back.
items.why: Both choices are good. Each helps different people, and each uses a source that comes back. Deciding means asking who gains most and who has been waiting longest.

items.p: Label a simple solar water heater with these words: Sun, black tank, cold water in, warm water out.
items.a: The Sun with rays on a flat black tank on a roof. Cold water going in at the bottom and warm water coming out at the top.
items.why: A black tank soaks up sunlight as heat, and the water takes the heat. Cold water goes in and warm water comes out, with no fuel burnt.
items.art: A blank outline of a roof, a flat black tank, a Sun and two pipes.

items.p: Which saves more energy in a day?
opts: Switching off a 9 watt bulb for 4 hours
They save the same, because both are off
Switching off a 60 watt fan for 4 hours
items.why: The fan saves 60 times 4, which is 240 watt-hours. The bulb saves 9 times 4, which is 36. The same time off saves more when the thing is hungrier.

items.p: A 50 watt fan runs for 8 hours. How many watt-hours of energy does it use?
items.why: 50 watts times 8 hours is 400 watt-hours. A unit on the electricity bill is 1,000 watt-hours.

worksheets.title: Taking, giving back and trading off (stretch)
worksheets.context: This sheet checks that you can test claims about renewable sources, follow coal back to its beginnings and weigh up the costs of different sources.

items.p: A pond gets 100 buckets of rain a month. A village takes 120 a month. Is the pond renewable for them?
opts: Not at this speed, because they take more than comes back
Yes, because rain comes every month
No, because the pond never fills with rain
items.why: The rain does fill the pond, but the village takes 20 buckets more than comes back each month. So the pond shrinks and one day runs dry. Renewable depends on the speed of taking, as the beans test showed.

items.p: Sort these by what they are made from.
cats: Made from beings who lived long ago
Made from beings who lived lately
items: Made from beings who lived long ago
Made from beings who lived lately
Made from beings who lived long ago
Made from beings who lived lately
Made from beings who lived long ago
Made from beings who lived lately
items.a: as given
items.why: Coal, oil and natural gas are fossil fuels made from beings buried millions of years ago. Wood, dung cakes and bagasse are biomass from plants and animals who lived recently.

items.p: Mala says, 'Taking 3 beans a round was safe, so cutting 3 trees a year is safe.' What is missing?
items.a: The 3 beans were what the game added each round. A real forest adds a different number each year. Mala needs to know how many trees grow back, and that changes with rain and land.
items.why: The safe number in the test came from the rule that 3 were added. A real forest has no such rule, so we must measure how fast it grows before saying a number is safe.

items.p: Bowl B gets 3 beans a round. If we take 4 beans a round, it will be empty in round 4.
items.why: False. Taking 4 and adding 3 makes the bowl fall by just one bean a round, so the bowl lasts until round 17. A small gap between the taking and the giving back is slow but still empties the bowl.

items.p: Put these in order, to show how coal forms.
items: black coal after millions of years
tall plants grow in a warm swamp
weight and heat press the plants into rock
the plants die and fall into the water
a: tall plants grow in a warm swamp
the plants die and fall into the water
weight and heat press the plants into rock
black coal after millions of years
items.why: Plants catch sunlight and grow. When they die in water, mud covers them before they rot. Weight and heat from the Earth press them over millions of years into coal.

items.p: Tidal power uses the rise and fall of the sea. Where does most of that energy come from?
opts: From the Sun, like the wind
From coal under the sea
From the pull of the Moon
items.why: The tides are raised mostly by the Moon's pull on the sea. That is one of the few sources not from the Sun.

items.p: Give one good thing and one problem about nuclear power.
items.a: Good: it adds almost no carbon dioxide, and a small amount of fuel gives a lot of energy. Problem: the used fuel stays dangerous for thousands of years, and uranium is not replaced.
items.why: A strong answer gives one real good thing and one real problem. Nuclear power is not renewable, since uranium is dug from mines, but nothing is burnt, so almost no carbon dioxide goes into the air.

items.p: Match each source to a real problem with it.
pairs: coal
smoke and carbon dioxide
a big dam
drowns a valley and blocks fish
a wind farm
needs land and its wires can kill birds
nuclear power
used fuel stays dangerous for thousands of years
items.a: as given
items.why: Every source costs something to someone. Knowing the cost lets families and countries weigh the choices, not just say clean or dirty.

items.p: A school has money for one of two things.

views.who: A headteacher who pays the bills (an imagined view)
views.says: Switch off lights and fans in empty rooms first. That costs nothing and cuts the bill straight away.

views.who: A student who likes science (an imagined view)
views.says: Put solar panels on the roof. They give electricity for years and show us how the Sun can run the school.

items.ask: Which would you do first, and could you do both?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer notes that saving costs nothing. Panels work best at a school that already wastes little. So both together are best.
items.why: Using less and making more are both good. Electricity that is saved does not have to be made, which is why many engineers say to save first.

items.p: An LED bulb of ____ watts gives as much light as an old bulb of 60 watts.
items.why: An LED of about 9 watts gives about as much light as an old 60 watt bulb. So six or seven LED bulbs can shine on the energy of one old bulb.

items.p: Four 60 watt bulbs become four 9 watt LEDs. Each runs 4 hours a day. How many watt-hours are saved daily?
items.why: Each bulb saves 60 minus 9, which is 51 watts. 51 times 4 hours is 204 watt-hours for one bulb. Four bulbs save 4 times 204, which is 816 watt-hours.

items.p: A friend says, 'Solar panels make energy from nothing.' What is a better way to say it?
items.a: Solar panels catch sunlight from the Sun and turn about 20 parts in every 100 of it into electricity. The rest becomes warmth.
items.why: A strong answer says where the energy comes from and does not claim it is made from nothing. A good panel today turns roughly 20 of every 100 parts of the sunlight into electricity.

items.p: A shopkeeper says, 'My solar panel keeps the fan running all night.' What is true?
opts: A battery must have stored the day's electricity
The panel stores sunlight in itself until night
The Moon gives the same light as the Sun
items.why: A panel makes electricity only while light falls on it. At night the energy must come from a battery or from the grid. The Moon only bounces back a little of the Sun's light and a panel gets almost no electricity from it.

items.p: Draw both bowls after 3 rounds. Take 2 beans from each, and add 3 to Bowl B. Write the beans in each.
items.a: Bowl A with 14 beans and Bowl B with 23 beans.
items.why: Bowl A loses 2 each round for 3 rounds, so 20 minus 6 leaves 14. Bowl B loses 2 and gains 3, so it gains 1 each round and has 23.
items.art: Two blank bowls drawn as circles on a page.

items.p: Three of these come back if we take them slowly enough. Which is the odd one out?
opts: Well water
Bamboo
Fish in a pond
Coal
items.why: A well, a bamboo clump and a fish pond all fill or grow again within years. Coal takes millions of years, so no family can wait for new coal.

worksheets.title: Speeds, stores and who pays (challenge)
worksheets.context: This sheet checks that you can use the two-speeds idea on new puzzles, weigh stores and costs, and explain a surprising result.

items.p: A well holds 300 buckets. Rain gives 40 a day, and a village takes 50. After how many days is it empty?
opts: 6 days
30 days
300 days
items.why: The well falls by 50 minus 40, which is 10 buckets each day. 300 divided by 10 is 30 days. A gap of just 10 a day is slow, so it is easy to miss until the end.

items.p: An iron of 1,000 watts is on for 15 minutes. How many watt-hours does it use?
items.why: 15 minutes is a quarter of an hour. A quarter of 1,000 watt-hours is 250.

items.p: Peat grows about 1 millimetre a year. A village digs 10 centimetres a year. Is peat renewable for them?
items.a: No. 10 centimetres is 100 millimetres, which is 100 times the growth. At that speed the peat runs out long before it can grow back.
items.why: The test is the same as the beans: compare the speed of taking with the speed of giving back. Peat does grow, so how fast we dig decides the answer.

items.p: India has coal for many years and wants cheaper electricity for every home.

views.who: An Indian energy planner (an imagined view)
views.says: Use our own coal now. Families need electricity today, and coal is steady.
Build solar and wind faster, because carbon dioxide stays in the air for a long time.

items.ask: What would you want to know before choosing, and could both be partly right?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer asks about cost, who gets power and how steady each source is. It may find that a mix is the answer.
items.why: Both views are serious. The choice depends on numbers that change every year, such as costs and how much electricity can be stored.

items.p: Nuclear power adds almost no carbon dioxide, so it has no problems.
items.why: False. Uranium is not renewable, and the used fuel stays dangerous for thousands of years. Keeping it safe for that long is still an open question.

items.p: Put these in order, from the newest sunlight to the oldest sunlight.
items: the wind that blew this morning
firewood from a tree that grew for 30 years
a: the wind that blew this morning
firewood from a tree that grew for 30 years
items.why: The wind is made from this week's sunlight. Rice caught sunlight over months and wood over decades. Coal holds sunlight caught long before the dinosaurs.

items.p: Uranium, used in nuclear power, was made by
opts: the Sun long ago
plants in swamps
exploding and colliding stars before the Sun was born
items.why: The Sun does not make uranium. Heavy atoms like uranium were made in exploding stars and in collisions of stars, long before the Sun and Earth formed.

items.p: Why is it wrong to say that coal is 'dead dinosaurs'?
items.a: Coal is mostly pressed plants from swamps, and much of it is older than the first dinosaurs. Oil is mostly tiny sea beings.
items.why: A strong answer says what coal really came from and does not claim dinosaurs were the main source. Coal formed from plants, and the biggest coal-forming forests grew before the first dinosaurs.

items.p: Match each real case to the bowl it behaves like.
pairs: a coal mine
Bowl A, where nothing is added
a well pumped less than the rain fills it
Bowl B, taking 2 beans a round
a forest cut faster than it grows
Bowl B, taking 6 beans a round
a bamboo clump cut once in 4 years
Bowl B, taking a small amount slowly
items.a: as given
items.why: The two bowls were models. A coal mine gets nothing back in a human lifetime, so it is like Bowl A. The other cases are like Bowl B, and the speed of taking decides if each lasts.

items.p: Three of these are ways to store energy for the evening. Which is the odd one out?
opts: A battery in an inverter
Water pumped up to a high lake
A heap of coal waiting for the power station
A solar panel on a roof
items.why: A battery, a high lake and a heap of coal all keep energy until it is used. A solar panel makes electricity while the Sun shines and does not keep any for night.

items.p: Choose one thing in your home that could use less energy without losing what your family needs. How would you do it?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer names a thing and gives a real change, such as a lid, an LED bulb or switching off in an empty room. It says roughly how much that would save.
items.why: Saving energy means getting the same light, cooking or travel from less. The best changes cost little and do not make anyone's day harder.

items.p: India made about 7 in 10 units from coal in about 2024, and it changes yearly. What is fair to say?
opts: India can switch off coal tomorrow
More stores and steady sources are needed as solar grows
Solar panels will never help
items.why: Solar works in daylight only. As it grows, India needs batteries, pumped water stores and other steady sources for evening and cloudy days. Coal cannot be switched off overnight, but the mix is changing.

items.p: Graph the beans in Bowl B for rounds 1 to 6, when 4 are taken and 3 are added each round.
items.a: Points at 19, 18, 17, 16, 15 and 14 beans, sliding down by one each round.
items.why: Bowl B loses 4 and gains 3, so it falls by one each round. A gentle slope can still end in an empty bowl, which a short test might not show.
items.art: A blank graph with rounds along the bottom and beans up the side.

items.p: Label a pumped storage station: high lake, low lake, turbine, water up at noon, water down at night.
items.a: A high lake and a low lake joined by a pipe with a turbine in it. An arrow up marked noon and an arrow down marked night.
items.why: At noon, spare electricity pumps water up. At night the water runs down through the turbine and makes electricity again. This is how a lake stores the Sun's work.
items.art: A blank picture of a high lake and a low lake joined by a pipe.

items.p: The amount of a fuel that people have found and can dig at a price worth paying is called its ____.
items.why: A reserve is always smaller than what is in the ground. New tools and higher prices make it larger, which is why the date for running out keeps moving.

quiz.p: Cooking gas in a cylinder is a fuel, and sunlight is not. Why?
opts: Gas is burnt for its stored energy, and sunlight is not burnt
Gas costs money and sunlight is free
Gas has more energy than sunlight
quiz.why: A fuel is something we burn to let out the energy stored in it. Sunlight is an energy source that nothing burns. If you chose the price, that tells us about shops and not about energy. Gas does not hold more energy than sunlight, since the Sun sends far more than we use.

quiz.p: A friend says power stations make energy. Which is a better way to say it?
opts: Power stations make energy out of nothing
Power stations only store energy for later
Power stations collect energy from a source and pass it on
quiz.why: Nobody makes energy out of nothing. A power station collects energy from coal, falling water, wind, sunlight or nuclear fuel and turns it into electricity. It is not mainly a store, because most of the energy leaves at once.

quiz.p: A village cuts 10 trees a year and 4 grow back. Is their firewood renewable?
opts: Yes, trees always grow back
Yes, because wood is a fuel
Not at this speed, because cutting is faster than growing
quiz.why: A source stays renewable only while we take from it more slowly than it comes back. This village takes 10 and gets back 4, so the forest shrinks each year. Trees do grow back, but not fast enough here. Being a fuel says nothing about coming back.

quiz.p: Peat grows about 1 millimetre a year. Why is it hard to put in one box?
opts: It grows back, but far slower than people dig it
It is not a fuel
It comes from the Sun
quiz.why: Peat is half-rotted swamp plants. It does grow, but very slowly, so people argue about whether to call it renewable. Peat does burn, so it is a fuel, and almost everything on Earth gets its energy from the Sun, so that does not decide the box.

quiz.p: Why is coal called a fossil fuel?
opts: It is dug from rocks under the ground
It is made from the buried remains of ancient living beings
It is as old as the dinosaur bones found with it
quiz.why: A fossil is a trace of ancient life kept in rock, and coal is made from the pressed bodies of swamp plants. Being dug from rock is true of many things that are not fossil fuels, such as iron ore. Coal is not tied to dinosaur bones, and much of it is older than the first dinosaurs.

quiz.p: A friend says oil came from dinosaurs. Which is better?
opts: Oil is dinosaur bodies pressed in rock
Most oil came from tiny sea beings
Oil was always in rocks and was never alive
quiz.why: Most oil began as tiny beings that floated near the sea surface, died and were buried in mud. Dinosaurs lived on land and in water, and their bodies are not the main source. Oil carries chemical marks of living beings, so it was not made without life.

quiz.p: A bowl gets 3 beans put back every round, and a player takes beans out every round. Which way of taking lets the bowl last?
opts: Taking 3 or fewer a round
Taking 5 a round
Taking 4 a round, because beans are left after 15 rounds
quiz.why: With 3 or fewer taken, Bowl B never shrinks, since 3 come back. Taking 5 empties it in round 10. Taking 4 leaves 5 beans at round 15, but it falls by one a round and is empty in round 17, so it only looks safe.

quiz.p: A bowl never gets any beans put back. If you take beans from it very slowly, what happens?
opts: It empties, only later
It never empties, because slow is safe
It fills up by itself
quiz.why: With nothing added, every bean taken is gone for good. Slower taking only makes the emptying later. Only a bowl that gets beans back can last. Coal is like Bowl A, because the adding is too slow for anyone to wait for.

quiz.p: A forest is cut faster than it grows. What is true about it?
opts: It can run out, because renewable depends on both speeds
It is still renewable, because trees grow
It is safe, because a forest is very big
quiz.why: Renewable is about how fast we take compared with how fast nature gives back. In the beans test, the same Bowl B lasted at one speed and ran out at another. A forest is not a bowl, but the same two speeds decide how long it lasts. Being big only makes the ending later.

quiz.p: What mainly makes the wind blow?
opts: The Sun warming land and sea unevenly
The Moon pulling the air
The Earth's inner heat
quiz.why: The Sun warms land faster than sea. Warm air rises and cooler air slides in under it, and that moving air is wind. The Moon pulls the sea into tides, and the Earth's inner heat is too small to drive the wind.

quiz.p: Which of these did not get its energy from the Sun?
opts: Uranium for nuclear power
Firewood
Coal
quiz.why: Firewood is sunlight caught by trees recently. Coal is sunlight caught by swamp plants long ago. The uranium atoms were made in exploding and colliding stars before the Sun was born.

quiz.p: A big dam gives clean electricity. Which is a real problem with it?
opts: It drowns a valley and blocks fish swimming upriver
It burns a lot of coal
It makes new coal under the water
quiz.why: A dam can flood forests, fields and villages, and a wall stops fish that swim upriver to lay eggs. It does not burn coal. No new coal forms in a lake behind a dam, since coal needs millions of years.

quiz.p: A solar panel alone cannot light a street at night. Why?
opts: Panels use up their own energy each day
Panels need light, so night needs a store such as a battery
Street lights only run on coal
quiz.why: A panel makes electricity only while light falls on it. To light a street at night we need a store, such as a battery, that was charged in the day. Panels do not use themselves up, and street lights can run on any source.

quiz.p: A 9 watt LED and a 60 watt bulb give equal light for 5 hours. How much more energy does the old one use?
opts: 255 watt-hours
51 watt-hours
300 watt-hours
quiz.why: The old bulb uses 60 times 5, which is 300 watt-hours. The LED uses 9 times 5, which is 45. The difference is 255. If you chose 51, you found the difference in watts and forgot the hours. If you chose 300, you gave the old bulb's total and did not subtract the LED's.

quiz.p: A city swaps to LED bulbs and still uses more electricity the next year. What is one possible reason?
opts: LED bulbs make more energy than they use
Cheaper light may mean more lights left on, or more things bought
Old bulbs always used less than LED bulbs
quiz.why: When something becomes cheaper to use, people sometimes use more of it, and the saving gets spent somewhere else. The English economist William Jevons noticed this about coal in 1865. No bulb makes energy, and an LED uses less than an old bulb for the same light.

applications: Your electricity bill shows units used. One unit is 1,000 watt-hours, which is a 1,000 watt iron on for an hour, or a 9 watt LED bulb on for about 110 hours. Find a bill, read the units, and ask which things at home used the most.

A cooking gas cylinder is a store of fuel. Ask how long the family's cylinder lasts. A lid on the pot can make it last longer. So can a pressure cooker, which uses about half the gas. Then fewer cylinders have to be made and carried.

A solar water heater on a roof catches sunlight as heat in a black tank. Look for one on a nearby building and notice the angle of the panel and which way it faces. In Bengaluru and Pune many roofs have one.

Count the people in the next bus you ride, and then count the cars beside it on the road with only one person inside. Ask how many cars the bus is standing in for, and how the road would look if every rider drove alone.
Think about a power cut at home. If you have an inverter, ask how many hours it keeps the lights on and which things you switch off to make it last. If you do not, ask what the neighbours use.
A village biogas tank turns dung and kitchen scraps into cooking gas, and the left-over slurry goes to the fields as manure. In Gujarat, Maharashtra and Tamil Nadu many families cook on gobar gas.

spotted.text: Look at the back of a ceiling fan, a bulb and a mixie. Find the number marked W. That is how many watts it uses. Notice that a mixie is far hungrier than a bulb, even though it runs for only a few minutes.
spotted.art: A hand holding a phone torch over a label on the back of a mixie.

spotted.text: Look at a lorry or a train of black coal as it goes along a railway or a harbour road. Notice how heavy it looks. That is old swamp sunlight on its way to a power station, perhaps from Odisha, Jharkhand or Telangana.
spotted.art: A goods train with open wagons full of black coal beside a station platform.

spotted.text: Look at an LPG cylinder in your kitchen. Notice the date stamp and how long it lasts. Ask how many times the family has bought one this year, and notice what makes it finish sooner, such as an open pot.
spotted.art: A gas cylinder with a stamped date and a stove beside it.

spotted.text: Look out for white wind turbines on a hill or a drive. If you pass them, count how many are spinning and how many are still. Notice that on a windy day nearly all spin together, and on a calm day nearly all stand still.
spotted.art: A row of white wind turbines on a hill, some turning and some still.
