spotted.text: Look at a roof or a street light with a solar panel. Notice which way it faces and if anything shades it. In India the panels face south, so that they catch the most sunlight through the day.
spotted.art: A solar street lamp beside a road with a small panel facing the Sun.

spotted.text: Look at clothes drying on a line, salt drying in pans or papad drying on a terrace. Notice that the Sun and the wind are doing work for free. Ask how much energy it would take to dry the same things on a stove.
spotted.art: A washing line of colourful clothes in the sun on a terrace.

spotted.text: At a petrol pump, look at the screen as the tank fills. Notice how many litres go in and how much it costs. A litre of petrol puts about 2.3 kilograms of carbon dioxide into the air when burnt.
spotted.art: A scooter at a petrol pump with a screen showing litres.

spotted.text: In a power cut, notice what runs on a battery and what stops. Ask how long the battery would last and what you could turn off to make it last longer.
spotted.art: A dark room with a small battery lamp and a family sitting on the floor.

ask_kids: Which of the things you used today came from the Sun a few months ago, and which came from the Sun a very long time ago?
If a river is renewable, can it still run dry? What would have to happen?
Would you rather live near a coal power station, a big dam or a solar park? What would you want to know first?
What is one thing in our home that we could use less, without missing it?
The Sun will shine for about 5 billion more years. Is there anything that is renewable for ever?

jokes.a: It was told it would be burnt out in the first few overs.

maths.problem: A well holds 200 buckets of water. Rain adds 30 buckets a day. A village takes 20, then 30, then 40 buckets a day. How many buckets are in the well after 10 days at each speed? How long until the 40 a day empties it?
maths.answer: After 10 days: 300 buckets at 20 a day, 200 at 30 a day and 100 at 40 a day. At 40 a day the well is empty in 20 days.
maths.explain: At 20 a day the well gains 30 minus 20, which is 10 each day, so 200 plus 100 is 300. At 30 a day nothing changes. At 40 a day it loses 10 each day, so 200 minus 100 is 100 after 10 days. 200 divided by 10 is 20 days to empty.
maths.context: This problem uses the same two speeds as the beans test, but with a well.
maths.why_maths: A source lasts or runs out depending on the gap between the speed of taking and the speed of giving back. That gap is a sum of change each day.

maths.problem: A 9 watt LED bulb and a 60 watt old bulb are each on for 5 hours a day. Work out the watt-hours for each in one day and in 30 days. How many units on the bill does the old bulb use more in 30 days? One unit is 1,000 watt-hours.
maths.answer: In one day, the LED uses 45 and the old bulb 300 watt-hours. In 30 days, 1,350 and 9,000. The old bulb uses 7.65 units more.
maths.explain: 9 times 5 is 45, and 60 times 5 is 300. Times 30 days: 45 times 30 is 1,350 and 300 times 30 is 9,000. 9,000 minus 1,350 is 7,650 watt-hours, which is 7.65 units.
maths.context: This problem works out how much a small change in watts adds up to on a bill over a month.
maths.why_maths: Energy used is power times time, so a small difference in watts becomes a big difference when it is multiplied by many hours.

maths.problem: On a rope of time, 1 centimetre stands for 1 million years. The coal swamps were 280 million years ago. The first people of our kind were 300,000 years ago. How far along the rope is each, and how many times farther is the coal than the people?
maths.answer: The coal is at 280 centimetres and the first people at 0.3 centimetre, which is 3 millimetres. The coal is roughly 930 times farther.
maths.explain: 280 million divided by 1 million is 280 centimetres. 300,000 divided by 1,000,000 is 0.3 centimetre. 280 divided by 0.3 is roughly 933.
maths.context: This problem uses the scale of the rope of time to compare how old coal is with how old our species is.
maths.why_maths: A scale turns very large times into lengths we can see and compare, which shows how out of proportion fast burning is to slow making.

warmup.q: Which is a fuel, a lump of coal or a gust of wind?
warmup.a: A lump of coal. A fuel is something we burn to let out its stored energy.
Able to be made new again. A renewable source comes back in days, seasons or a few years.

warmup.q: What is the Sun's job for the wind?
warmup.a: The Sun warms land and sea unequally. Warm air rises, cooler air moves in, and the moving air is wind.

warmup.q: Which three fuels are fossil fuels?
warmup.a: Coal, oil and natural gas. They are made from the buried remains of ancient living beings.

warmup.q: What is a unit on an electricity bill?
warmup.a: 1,000 watt-hours, such as a 1,000 watt iron on for an hour.

warmup.q: Name one thing that can be renewable and still run out.
warmup.a: A forest, a well or a fishpond, if we take from it faster than it comes back.

quiz: Coal, oil and natural gas are made from the buried remains of ancient living beings.
Coal began as swamp plants, and oil and gas as tiny sea beings, buried and pressed over millions of years.
A renewable source can never run out, however fast we take from it.
A source lasts only while we take more slowly than nature gives back. A well or a forest can run out.
Most oil came from dinosaurs.
Most oil came from tiny sea beings who sank into mud.
Wind is made by the Sun warming land and sea unequally.
Warm air rises, cooler air slides in under it, and that moving air is wind.
Uranium for nuclear power got its energy from the Sun.
The Sun did not make uranium. It was made in stars that ended before the Sun formed.
A solar panel makes some electricity at night from the dark.
A panel needs light. At night the energy must come from a battery or the grid.
Using less energy is a way of making a source last longer.
Every bit of energy not used is fuel that stays in the ground, or a source that has time to recover.
A big dam has no cost, because the water comes back every year.
A big dam can drown a valley, block fish and move villages, even though the rain comes back.
A lid on a pot of water makes it boil sooner.
The lid keeps the heat in, so the water warms faster and less gas is needed.
Sunlight that fell on a coal swamp 280 million years ago is still in the coal.
The plants caught it and stored it. Burning the coal lets it out as heat and light.
odd: Coal, oil and natural gas are fossil fuels from ancient beings. Firewood comes from trees that grew in recent years.
Wind, rain and sunlight all come from the Sun's work. Uranium was made in stars before the Sun was born.
A solar cooker, a solar panel and a wind turbine collect energy from the Sun or the wind. A battery only stores energy collected elsewhere.
A dam, a pipe and a turbine are all parts of a water power station. A coal heap belongs to a coal station.
Biogas, firewood and dung cakes are made from beings who lived recently. Petrol is made from oil, from ancient sea beings.
